newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Mayne seen making weak profit.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Mayne seen making weak profit.

text.p: Australian transport, logistics and health group Mayne Nickless Ltd is forecast to report another weak half-year net profit on Thursday, but analysts say a single investment clouds the company's outlook.

Mayne is expected to post a net profit before abnormals of between A$47.5 million and about A$50 million for the six months to December 31, according to the forecasts of stock analysts contacted by Reuters.
This is a little weaker than the A$55.3 million reported a year ago, but marks a return to growth from the A$29.8 million in the previous half year.
Mayne's annual net profit for 1996/97 (July/June) is predicted on average to rise 14 percent to A$97 million from a dismal 1995/96, according to a Barceps forecasting survey.
Mayne's health care division, which has emerged as its star performer, will again post strong earnings in the first half, but the express freight business is struggling, analysts said.
The logistics division, which manages flows of goods from the factory to points of consumption, is also meeting some difficulties, a Sydney-based analyst said.
"They have a lot of sensitivities to the retail sector and particularly to the apparel sector," the analyst said.

Australia's retail sector has been hit hard by a prolonged slump in consumer spending, with apparel sales among the worst affected. The logistics division is also weighed down by its underperforming Belgian business, Heijden Logistics.
Analysts said they were optimistic about Mayne's profit outlook and saw a pick-up in 1997/98, especially on the transport side, as the domestic economy gathered pace.
But they said Mayne's failure so far to exit its 25 percent stake in Optus Communications was a concern.
Mayne's stake in the telecommunications carrier is estimated to be worth around A$1 billion -- cash Mayne needs to retire debt and fund the planned expansion of its health care business.
Mayne has said it wants to sell its stake as part of the planned float of Optus, but legal action involving an Optus associate, pay television firm Optus Vision, has stalled this.
"At the moment their share price is being bashed by this uncertainty because of the Optus litigation," said analyst Justin Arter of brokerage J.B. Were & Son.
"I think it (the stock) is undervalued, but I can't forecast litigation any better than you can."
Another Sydney-based analyst agreed, noting the interest payments associated with the Optus stake were a drag on profits.

"It's really quite a noose around their neck. Until that thing is sold, they can't get their cash and they still have to carry the debt and still have to carry interest costs. It's a fairly simple story," he said.
